newsitem.title: INDIA: FOCUS - Debt mountain casts shadow over India economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Debt mountain casts shadow over India economy.

text.p: India, squeezed by a steep interest rate regime and increased government borrowing, appears to be marching into a domestic debt trap, economic analysts said on Sunday.
This could affect the nation's economic growth and possibly interrupt a five-year-old economic reform programme, they said after a stern warning to the government from the central bank last week.

The Reserve Bank of India said in its annual report on the economy released on Friday that the government's total domestic liabilities at the end of March stood at a high 58.8 percent of gross domestic product.
Economists said that high interest rates, increased market borrowing by the government and rising government expenditure were factors responsible for pushing the economy into a debt trap.
"We are going into a debt trap and the fiscal situation is worsening," S.P. Gupta, director of the independent Indian Council for Research in International Economic Relations, told Reuters.
But Finance Minister P. Chidambaram dismissed such fears when he spoke to a conference of bankers on Friday.
"The debt is high but not alarming," he said, adding that high economic growth and increased tax revenue would help the government to meet its domestic debt obligations.
Analysts said that the nation was close to plunging into a vicious circle of borrowing more and more from the market to meet its interest payment obligations.

Interest payments eat up nearly half of government revenues. India's interest payments in 1996/97 (April-March) are estimated to rise to 600 billion rupees ($16.8 billion) against 520 billion in 1995/96.
The RBI said the growth of interest payments must be arrested to lower debt obligations.
"What is crucial is, however, to generate adequate primary surplus which could meet the entire debt service obligation," the central bank said.

Gupta, a former adviser to the Indian government's economic planning body, said the government was borrowing more to meet current payments, such as salaries, and not using the funds to build productive assets.
"This pushes up the fiscal deficit," Gupta said.
Fiscal deficit is the sum of the budgetary deficit and total government borrowings.
"The fiscal situation poses a major challenge. The deficits have to be brought down," V. Raghuraman, secretary-general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters.
India aims to lower its fiscal deficit to 5.0 percent of GDP in 1996/97 against 5.7 percent in 1995/96.
"The way out of this debt trap is to sell off stakes in state-owned companies and use the proceeds to retire (pay back) a portion of the public debt," Gupta said.
India, which began a partial privatisation programme in 1991/92, aims to raise 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion) from a disinvestment programme in 1996/97.
"There is some thinking in the government to put a cap on public debt," a financial ministry official, who asked not be identified, told Reuters.
A ceiling would force the government to improve its fiscal position and borrow more prudently, the official said.
($1 = 35.7 rupees)
